_comment: The AWS environment's single source of truth - the same role clusters/onprem/nodes.json plays
for the laptop and clusters/gcp/cluster.json plays for GKE (ADR-0008). Every value that could
disagree with reality comes from here, so it cannot disagree.
REWRITTEN 2026-11-05. The first version of this file described an EKS cluster with a managed
node group, and docs/roadmap.md asks for the opposite: 'AWS: the self-managed environment -
Terraform for spot EC2 instances (no NAT gateway); Ansible reused from Module 03 to build the
cluster'. ADR-0022's amendment records how that happened. The EKS session the roadmap does
want is one comparison run at the end of the module, not the substrate.
WHICH ACCOUNT, and it is not the one with the credits. 730335198894 is activated and has no
credit balance; 331970435482 has $100 and has been stuck on OptInRequired since sign-up with a
support case open. ADR-0003 Decision 6 records why running on real money is the better trade
rather than merely the available one. THE ACCOUNT ID IS NOT IN THIS FILE: it is not a
credential, but this repository is public and it identifies a payment instrument. The API
supplies it, and `make aws-guardrails` prints the account it is about to act on.
_az_comment: ONE AZ, AND THAT IS NOW A CHOICE RATHER THAN A CONSTRAINT. The EKS version of this file said
two AZs were forced, which is true of an EKS control plane and false of kubeadm on plain EC2.
One AZ because cross-AZ traffic is billed per GB in both directions, and a three-node cluster
gossiping across zones would pay for every etcd heartbeat. The honest consequence, stated
rather than discovered: THIS CLUSTER IS NOT HIGHLY AVAILABLE. Neither is the GKE one, and
neither is the laptop. Availability is Module 11's subject, not a property to claim here.
1a $0.0269 - all within a rupee of each other, so this is about capacity rather than price.
AZ NAMES ARE PER-ACCOUNT ALIASES: ap-south-1b on this account is not necessarily the same
physical zone as ap-south-1b on another, so this pin is account-specific and so is that
price. If a spot request cannot be filled, change this one value and re-apply:
_cluster_name_comment: `platform`, the same name as the GKE cluster and the on-prem one, deliberately. The kubectl
CONTEXT is what must differ: `make aws-kubeconfig` names it `aws-platform`, to sit beside
`gcp-platform` and `onprem-admin` without any of the three being a prefix of another.
_kubernetes_comment: THE SAME MINOR AS ON-PREM, and this is the one version pin in this project that can actually
be held across substrates. The laptop runs v1.34.12 from the Packer image; GKE runs v1.36.4
and cannot be pinned at all (parking lot, 2026-11-01), which is what 'managed' means.
This value is K8S_MINOR in packer/ubuntu-2404/scripts/30-kubernetes.sh, which pins the
pkgs.k8s.io repository and then `apt-mark hold`s kubelet, kubeadm and kubectl. Two of three
substrates therefore run the same Kubernetes, which makes the GKE gap a measurement rather
EVERY VALUE HERE IS A COPY OF ONE IN clusters/onprem/nodes.json, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE WITH
A CHECK RATHER THAN CLEVER WITHOUT ONE. Having the AWS inventory read the on-prem file would
remove the duplication and create a worse problem - an AWS build failing because somebody
edited the laptop's config - which is the coupling ADR-0008 exists to avoid: each substrate's
file is the truth for that substrate. So they are duplicated and `make lint` fails if they
stop agreeing, the same arrangement as the GCP secret backend whose overlay repeats the
project and cluster names because Argo CD cannot reach into a JSON file.
WHAT IS NOT COPIED: the Argo CD pins, which live in clusters/platform.json for all three
_budget_comment: ADR-0003 Decision 3: this exists BEFORE the first resource, in its own Terraform state, with
its own make target. A guardrail applied in the same run as the thing it guards is not a
$5 IS SIZED AGAINST ONE FORGOTTEN NIGHT, not picked for roundness. Three nodes and a load
balancer left overnight is about $1.70, so 50% of $5 fires the next morning - which is when
an alert is useful. A $50 budget on a lab that runs three hours a week never fires, and an
alarm that never fires is indistinguishable from no alarm.
CURRENCY IS UNVERIFIED FOR THIS ACCOUNT. An AWS Budget is rejected rather than converted if
its currency is not the account's billing currency. 730335198894 is an older Indian account
and may bill in INR. Check Billing -> Bills before the first apply; if it is INR, change both
values here together - 400 INR keeps it the same size as the GCP guardrail rather than a
_addresses_comment: THE PRIVATE ADDRESSES ARE DECLARED, NOT ALLOCATED - which is a change made on 2026-11-05
after preflight refused to build the cluster:
Some node names do not resolve: ['aws-cp01', 'aws-w01', 'aws-w02'].
controlPlaneEndpoint is a NAME, so a node that cannot resolve it cannot join.
On the laptop, clusters/onprem/nodes.json declares each address and cloud-init writes
/etc/hosts from it, so every node resolves every other by name. The first AWS version let
EC2 allocate addresses at launch, which meant Terraform could not know them when it rendered
the user-data - so nothing could write /etc/hosts, and the nodes knew each other only by
Declaring them makes the two substrates the same shape AND makes a rebuild deterministic:
aws-cp01 is 10.20.1.10 today and after the next `make aws-up`, so a kubeconfig or a note in
a runbook does not go stale.
WHY .10 AND NOT .1: AWS RESERVES THE FIRST FOUR ADDRESSES AND THE LAST ONE in every subnet -
.0 network, .1 the VPC router, .2 DNS, .3 reserved for the future, .255 broadcast. Asking for
one of those fails the apply with a message about an address being unavailable, which reads
like a conflict with something else. Starting at .10 leaves the reserved block alone and
keeps room to grow without renumbering.
_nodes_comment: THREE NODES, MIRRORING ON-PREM: one control plane and two workers, named aws-cp01, aws-w01
and aws-w02 against the laptop's k8s-cp01, k8s-w01 and k8s-w02. The names ARE settable here,
unlike GKE where they come from the managed instance group - which is itself one of the six
differences ADR-0001 asks Module 09 to produce.
Two nodes would carry ShopVerse (the on-prem control plane is schedulable and the smoke test
runs a pod on it), and would save about a third. Three is chosen anyway: node-count parity
with the laptop is most of what makes the comparison a comparison.
m6a.large: 2 DEDICATED vCPU, 8 GB. NOT t3.large, NOT t3.medium, and this is the comment to
read before 'saving money' here.
THE t3 FAMILY IS BURSTABLE - a baseline fraction of a vCPU plus credits - and the Kubernetes
scheduler schedules against neither. That is the same trap as GCP's e2-medium, which is
listed as 2 vCPU, guarantees one, reported 940m allocatable, and made ADR-0016's capacity
estimate wrong by 2.05x: six of ShopVerse's eight pods stayed Pending with 'Insufficient
cpu', and MongoDB's PVC stayed Pending behind them.
The failure shape is why this is a pin rather than a measurement: A BURSTABLE NODE DOES NOT
FAIL AT CREATION. It creates, reports Ready, and then refuses to schedule - so the symptom
arrives one layer away from the cause, inside the tenant's Application.
VERIFIED 2026-11-05, by asking the API rather than reading a blog:
aws ec2 describe-instance-type-offerings --region ap-south-1 \
--filters Name=instance-type,Values=m6a.large --query 'InstanceTypeOfferings[].Location'
-> ap-south-1
It carried an explicit UNVERIFIED note from the day it was written until that ran, because
three pins in this repository have been wrong from memory. scripts/aws-account-probe.sh asks
it on every run, so a region change re-tests it without anybody remembering to.
SPOT, for the ~72% discount measured on 2026-11-05 ($0.0266 against on-demand), and with the
trade that an instance can be reclaimed at two minutes' notice. Module 11 uses that
deliberately. Losing the CONTROL PLANE to a reclaim is a different event from losing a worker
and this cluster has no answer for it - which is a thing to know before relying on a session,
not a thing to discover during one.
MAX PODS PER NODE IS AN AWS-ONLY CEILING when the VPC CNI is used, because each pod takes a
real VPC IP from an ENI. THIS CLUSTER DOES NOT USE THE VPC CNI - it runs the same Cilium the
laptop runs, from the same Ansible role, with pod addresses from an overlay. So the ceiling
does not apply, and that is precisely the kind of difference the module exists to surface:
the constraint is a property of the CNI, not of AWS.
_ssh_comment: THE SAME KEY FILE clusters/onprem/nodes.json names, so one key reaches all three substrates
and Ansible needs no per-substrate credential. Stated here rather than read from the on-prem
file: each substrate's config is the source of truth for that substrate (ADR-0008), and a
cross-read would make the AWS build fail if the laptop's file changed.
`ubuntu` is Canonical's default user on their AMIs - the on-prem image uses a user the
cloud-init seed creates, which is a difference Ansible absorbs through the inventory.
_image_comment: THE SAME IMAGE DEFINITION AS ON-PREM, DELIVERED DIFFERENTLY, and the difference is the
interesting part (ADR-0025).
On-prem, packer/ubuntu-2404/scripts/ bakes a golden image and ansible/roles/preflight ASSERTS
that it did its job - it never changes a host (ADR-0008). On a bare Ubuntu AMI every one of
those assertions fails, because kubeadm and containerd are not there.
Three ways out, and the cost rule picks one:
a Packer AMI for AWS   mirrors on-prem exactly, and an AMI is a standing EBS snapshot
charge, which ADR-0003 Decision 2 forbids. Deregistering and
rebuilding each session is ~10 minutes every session.
relax preflight        breaks ADR-0008. No.
cloud-init at boot     the SAME scripts, run at first boot. Zero standing cost, ~2 minutes,
and preflight keeps asserting honestly - it now asserts that
cloud-init did the job rather than that Packer did.
owner 099720109477 is Canonical's. The AMI ID is deliberately NOT pinned here: it changes
with every Ubuntu point release, a stale ID fails the apply with a message about an image
rather than about a pin, and the thing being held constant is the SCRIPTS, not the base.
099720109477 is the one value in this file nobody can verify by reading it. Check it once:
aws ec2 describe-images --owners 099720109477 --region ap-south-1 \
--filters 'Name=name,Values=ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd-gp3/ubuntu-noble-24.04-amd64-server-*' \
--query 'sort_by(Images,&CreationDate)[-1].[ImageId,Name,OwnerId]' --output text
_networking_comment: PUBLIC SUBNET WITH PUBLIC IPs ON THE NODES, which looks wrong and is the same decision the
GKE cluster made for the same reason (ADR-0019 Decision 3).
ShopVerse's seven images are on ghcr.io, and the nodes also need pkgs.k8s.io and
archive.ubuntu.com at first boot for the cloud-init provisioning above. ADR-0003 forbids NAT
gateways - at roughly $0.045/hour plus per-GB processing, a NAT gateway is the most expensive
idle object in either cloud - and a node in a private subnet with no NAT reaches none of
those. VPC endpoints cover AWS's own APIs and nothing else, exactly as Private Google Access
So: a public subnet, public IPs, and SECURITY GROUPS as the boundary. A public IPv4 address
is $0.005/hour each since 2024 EVEN WHEN ATTACHED, which is ₹1.35/hour for three and the
other reason ADR-0003's target reads '₹0 steady-state' rather than '₹0 ever'.
pod_cidr and service_cidr MATCH THE LAPTOP (clusters/onprem/nodes.json) on purpose, and they
are deliberately outside vpc_cidr. Cilium gives pods addresses from an overlay rather than
from the VPC, so these never need to be routable in AWS - which is what lets the same numbers
serve both substrates. 10.96.0.0/12 overlapping nothing in 10.20.0.0/16 is the property that
ONE SUBNET, not one per AZ, because there is one AZ - see _az_comment.
